lessons.title: The Indian Valuation Rulebook: Registered Valuers, Rule 11UA and FEMA Pricing

children.text: In the last lesson, valuation was a negotiation. In India, it is also a legal document. Before a private company can issue shares to you, a registered professional has usually signed a valuation report. If a foreign investor is involved, a second rulebook sets a minimum price. And when you buy shares from someone else, the tax department has its own idea of what those shares are worth. This lesson walks through the three regimes that put rupee figures on startup shares, and the practical traps each one creates for investors.

body.text: A startup share in India can have three official values at once: one for company law, one for foreign exchange rules and one for income tax. None of them is the price you negotiated, and each can matter to your deal.

Section and rule numbers for income tax in this lesson refer to the Income-tax Act, 1961 and the Income-tax Rules, 1962, because most valuation reports, agreements and articles still use them. The Income-tax Act, 2025 applies from 1 April 2026 and renumbers these provisions. Confirm current references with a chartered accountant.

children.text: Regime 1: Company Law and the Registered Valuer

When an unlisted company issues new shares to specific investors, it is making a preferential allotment under Section 62(1)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013, usually through the private placement process in Section 42. Three requirements matter to you as an investor.
A valuation report.
The price must be supported by a report from a
registered valuer

markDefs.definition: A professional registered with the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India under the Companies (Registered Valuers and Valuation) Rules, 2017, for asset classes such as securities or financial assets.

children.text: A special resolution.
Shareholders must approve the issue, with at least 75% of votes cast in favour.
An offer letter and a filing.
Investors receive a private placement offer letter in Form PAS-4, and the company files the return of allotment in Form PAS-3 with the Registrar of Companies once shares are allotted.

body.label: IBBI: Registered Valuers
body.description: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India maintains the register of registered valuers. Check that the valuer who signed a startup's report is actually registered for securities or financial assets.

body.text: A registered valuer's report is not due diligence. For a young startup, the valuer typically runs a DCF on projections supplied by the founders. If the founders forecast ₹100 crore of revenue in five years, the report will usually reflect it. The report proves a process was followed, not that the price is sensible.

children.text: Regime 2: FEMA Pricing for Foreign and NRI Money

The moment a person resident outside India invests, the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 apply. Their pricing guidelines protect India from capital leaving the country too cheaply, and they work in one direction at a time.

body.caption: FEMA pricing guidelines for unlisted Indian companies

cells: Company issues new shares to a non-resident
Chartered accountant, SEBI-registered merchant banker or practising cost accountant, using an internationally accepted pricing method on an arm's length basis
Resident sells existing shares to a non-resident
Non-resident sells existing shares to a resident
Conversion price or formula fixed upfront; price at conversion not lower than fair value at the time of issue

stats.label: Report a new share issue to a non-resident
stats.context: Form FC-GPR, from the date of issue

stats.label: Report a transfer between resident and non-resident
stats.context: Form FC-TRS, from receipt or remittance of funds

stats.label: Where both are filed
stats.context: RBI's reporting platform, through the company's bank

body.text: FEMA quietly limits downside protection for foreign investors. Because CCPS issued to a non-resident cannot convert at a price below fair value at issue, an aggressive anti-dilution clause that would cut the conversion price in a down round may not be fully enforceable for them. Chapter 4 returns to this.

children.text: One useful exception for Indian investors abroad: investments by an NRI or OCI on a non-repatriation basis are treated as domestic investment, so the FEMA pricing floor and foreign investment reporting generally do not apply to them. Money invested on a repatriation basis, which can later be taken out of India freely, follows the full rules.

body.title: Selling to an NRI
body.question: Sneha, a Pune resident, holds equity shares in an unlisted startup. The certified fair value is ₹480 per share. Her cousin in Singapore, investing on a repatriation basis, offers to buy them at ₹450. What does FEMA say?
options: The sale is fine because both parties agreed the price
The price must be at least ₹480 because a resident is selling to a non-resident
The price must be at most ₹480 because the buyer is a non-resident
FEMA does not apply to transfers between relatives
body.explanation: When a resident sells to a non-resident, the price cannot be less than fair value, so ₹450 is not allowed. The rule stops shares, and therefore value, from leaving India below their worth. The reverse transfer, from a non-resident to a resident, is capped at fair value instead.

children.text: Regime 3: Income Tax and Rule 11UA
Rule 11UA
tells you how to calculate fair market value for tax. It has mattered in two very different ways, one of which has now ended.

markDefs.definition: The rule under the Income-tax Rules, 1962 that sets out how to calculate the fair market value of shares and other property for income tax purposes.

children.text: The angel tax era, now over

From 2012, Section 56(2)(viib) taxed a closely held company when it issued shares at a price above fair market value. The excess premium was treated as the company's income, which is why it became known as angel tax. It caused years of disputes for startups, eased only partly by an exemption for DPIIT-recognised startups.

body.title: The rise and fall of angel tax

events.title: Angel tax introduced
events.description: Section 56(2)(viib) taxes share premium above fair market value when a closely held company issues shares to resident investors.

events.title: Startup exemption
events.description: DPIIT-recognised startups meeting prescribed conditions become eligible for exemption. The same year, FEMA pricing moves into the new Non-Debt Instruments Rules.

events.title: Extended to foreign investors
events.description: The Finance Act, 2023 extends angel tax to non-resident investors, and Rule 11UA is amended to allow more valuation methods and a 10% tolerance band.

events.title: Abolition announced
events.description: Union Budget 2024-25 abolishes angel tax for all classes of investors. Section 56(2)(viib) is omitted for share issues from financial year 2024-25 onwards.

events.title: New Income-tax Act
events.description: The Income-tax Act, 2025 comes into force, replacing the 1961 Act and renumbering its provisions.

body.title: Why founders called it the "valuation sandwich"

children.text: Before 2024, a startup raising money from a foreign investor could be squeezed between two rules pointing in opposite directions.
FEMA set a floor.
Shares issued to the foreign investor could not be priced below fair value.
Angel tax set a ceiling.
Any price above fair market value under Rule 11UA could be taxed as income of the company.

With two valuations prepared under different rules by different professionals, the room between the floor and the ceiling could be very narrow. The 2023 amendments added a 10% tolerance to help, and the 2024 abolition of angel tax removed the ceiling for new issues. The FEMA floor still applies.
The rule that still bites investors: buying below fair market value

Angel tax is gone, but Section 56(2)(x) is not. It taxes the buyer. If you receive shares for less than their fair market value, and the gap is more than ₹50,000, the entire gap is taxed as your income from other sources, at your slab rate.

body.latex: \text{Deemed income} = (\text{FMV per share} - \text{Price paid per share}) \times \text{Number of shares}, \text{ if above } ₹50{,}000
body.caption: Taxable in full once the gap exceeds ₹50,000

children.text: For unquoted equity shares, Rule 11UA calculates fair market value for this purpose using a formula based on the company's adjusted book value. For a loss-making startup, that number can be far below the price investors paid in the last round. For preference shares such as CCPS, fair market value is broadly the price the shares would fetch if sold in the open market, usually supported by a valuation report.

body.label: The seller is affected too
body.context: When unquoted shares are sold below fair market value, the seller's capital gains are generally calculated as if they received fair market value. A cheap sale can create tax on both sides of the same transaction.

children.text: Worked Example: One Share, Three Values

SolarSaathi Energy Private Limited is a fictional Ahmedabad startup selling rooftop solar on EMI to small businesses. It raises a round from Indian angels and a Singapore fund at ₹500 per equity share.

body.caption: The values attached to one SolarSaathi equity share (illustrative)

cells: Minimum price for the Singapore fund

children.text: The round is compliant: ₹500 is above the ₹480 FEMA fair value, so the Singapore fund pays enough, and since the share issue happens after angel tax was abolished, pricing above fair market value creates no tax for SolarSaathi.
Now Rohit, a Surat angel who missed the round, buys 2,000 equity shares from a departing early employee at ₹150 per share. The Rule 11UA fair market value is ₹180.

Had Rohit paid ₹160 per share, the gap would have been ₹20 × 2,000 = ₹40,000, below the threshold, and nothing would have been taxable under this provision. The seller, meanwhile, would generally compute capital gains as if they had received ₹180 per share.

body.title: Deemed income on a discount deal
body.prompt: An investor buys 5,000 unquoted equity shares at ₹165 each. The Rule 11UA fair market value is ₹180 per share. How much is taxable as the investor's income under Section 56(2)(x), in ₹?
body.explanation: Gap = (₹180 - ₹165) × 5,000 = ₹75,000. This is more than ₹50,000, so the entire ₹75,000 is taxable as income from other sources, not just the amount above ₹50,000.

body.title: The FEMA floor
body.textWithBlank: Under FEMA pricing guidelines, an unlisted Indian company cannot issue shares to a person resident outside India at a price ___ fair value.
body.explanation: Fair value, certified by a chartered accountant, SEBI-registered merchant banker or practising cost accountant, sets the minimum price for issues to non-residents.

children.text: What This Means When You Invest

columns.label: Companies Act
points: Applies to: every preferential allotment by an unlisted company
Your check: ask for the report and PAS-4

columns.label: FEMA
points: Applies to: any non-resident investor on a repatriation basis
Valued by: CA, SEBI-registered merchant banker or cost accountant
Direction: floor on issues and inbound transfers, cap on outbound transfers
Your check: FC-GPR or FC-TRS filed on time

columns.label: Income tax
points: Applies to: buyers receiving shares below fair market value, and sellers under Section 50CA
Direction: taxes the gap if above ₹50,000
Your check: FMV before any discounted secondary purchase

body.title: The shortcut offer from Dubai
body.scenario: Arjun, an NRI engineer in Dubai, wants to invest ₹25 lakh in a Kochi startup run by a school friend. The founder suggests: "Skip the paperwork. Transfer the money to my personal account from your NRE account. I'll sell you some of my own shares at ₹200 when the round is done. The fund is paying ₹600, so you're getting a great deal."
body.prompt: List the regulatory and tax problems with this proposal, and what Arjun should do instead.
body.modelAnswer:
Problems:
1. Money to the founder, not the company. Paying a founder personally is not an investment in the startup. There is no allotment, no PAS-3 filing and no record that Arjun owns anything until a transfer is completed.
2. FEMA pricing. Money from an NRE account is a repatriation-basis investment. A resident founder selling shares to Arjun must price them at or above fair value. If fair value is anywhere near the ₹600 round price, ₹200 breaches the floor.
3. FEMA reporting. A transfer from a resident to a non-resident must be reported in Form FC-TRS within 60 days. "Skipping the paperwork" is not an option.
4. Tax on the buyer. If the Rule 11UA fair market value exceeds ₹200 and the total gap exceeds ₹50,000, Arjun has deemed income under Section 56(2)(x).
5. Tax on the seller. The founder's capital gains would generally be computed on fair market value under Section 50CA, not the ₹200 received.

What Arjun should do:
1. Invest directly in the company's round, at the round price, and receive shares by allotment with proper PAS-4, PAS-3 and FC-GPR filings.
2. Or, if he wants lighter FEMA requirements, consider investing on a non-repatriation basis from an NRO account after taking advice, understanding that the money cannot then be freely taken out of India.
3. Get a CA to confirm fair value and tax exposure before any secondary purchase.

body.title: Valuation paperwork to request before you invest
steps: The registered valuer's report supporting the issue price, and the valuer's IBBI registration.
The private placement offer letter (Form PAS-4) addressed to you.
The special resolution approving the allotment.
If any investor is non-resident: the FEMA fair value certificate and confirmation that Form FC-GPR will be filed within 30 days.
After allotment: a copy of Form PAS-3 as filed with the Registrar of Companies.
For any secondary purchase: a Rule 11UA fair market value calculation before you agree a price.

cards.definition: A professional registered with IBBI whose report supports the price of a preferential allotment under the Companies Act.
The private placement offer letter sent to identified investors.
The value, certified by a CA, merchant banker or cost accountant, that sets the price floor for issuing shares to non-residents.
The RBI report filed within 30 days of issuing shares to a non-resident.
The RBI report filed within 60 days for a share transfer between a resident and a non-resident.
The former tax under Section 56(2)(viib) on share premium above fair market value, abolished from financial year 2024-25.
Taxes a buyer who receives shares below fair market value, when the gap exceeds ₹50,000.
Treats fair market value as the sale price for a seller of unquoted shares sold below that value.

points: A preferential allotment by an unlisted company needs a registered valuer's report, a special resolution, a PAS-4 offer letter and a PAS-3 filing.
A valuation report proves a process was followed. It usually rests on founder projections and is not a substitute for your own judgement.
FEMA sets a floor on issues and inbound transfers to non-residents and a cap on outbound transfers, with FC-GPR and FC-TRS reporting.
Angel tax under Section 56(2)(viib) has been abolished for share issues from financial year 2024-25.
Buying shares below Rule 11UA fair market value can still create taxable income for the buyer under Section 56(2)(x), and affects the seller under Section 50CA.
Income tax section numbers have changed under the Income-tax Act, 2025. Confirm current references with a chartered accountant.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. SolarSaathi and all individuals named are fictional. Valuation, FEMA and tax rules are detailed, change often and have exceptions not covered here. Consult a chartered accountant, a lawyer and a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
